stem: New growth develops an apparent micronutrient-related chlorosis while root-zone pH has drifted substantially from the intended range. What is the most defensible first hypothesis to test?
choices: Availability may be impaired by root-zone conditions even if the micronutrient is present in the feed
The micronutrient concentration in the fertilizer is probably too low because visible chlorosis is more diagnostic than the root-zone pH change
The symptom likely reflects a stable genetic expression pattern because new-growth chlorosis is less sensitive to short-term root-zone chemistry
The pH drift may affect solution stability, but micronutrient uptake is generally controlled independently enough that supply should be checked first
rationale: Micronutrient symptoms can reflect availability rather than simple absence. Root-zone pH and other conditions should be checked before concluding that supply is missing.
